section_summary: Pages 161–203 continue Bulletin No. 19 of the Chinese Council for Economic Research, a statistical study of Japan’s dependence on foreign sources—especially the United States and the British Empire—for petroleum, metals, machinery, vehicles, aircraft, and other materials essential to war. The report evaluates the effect of the European war, the American “moral embargo,” export licensing, and a possible comprehensive embargo, followed by extensive commodity and country tables for 1937–1940. Pages 204–216 contain State Department and congressional correspondence concerning the bulletin and public protests against scrap-metal, steel-rail, and aviation-gasoline shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: World Exports to Japan Essential for War Purposes, 1937–39 (Bulletin No. 19)
subfiles.about: Analyzes Japan’s foreign procurement of commodities and equipment needed for war and the strategic leverage held by the United States.
subfiles.summary: The report traces changes in Japan’s 1937–1939 imports of petroleum, scrap iron, copper, machine tools, vehicles, aircraft, ferro-alloys, and other strategic goods, identifying the United States as the dominant supplier. It examines supplies from Canada, European countries, colonial Asia, and Oceania, then argues that wartime disruption and American export controls placed Japan’s military economy in a precarious position. Charts and extensive appendices provide country and commodity values, quantities, percentage shares, and comparisons through the first half of 1940.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Chinese Council Bulletin No. 19
subfiles.from: Stuart J. Fuller, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Thanks the Chinese ambassador for providing a copy of the council’s bulletin on war-essential exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Fuller acknowledges Chinese Council Bulletin No. 19 on world exports to Japan and looks forward to reading it.

subfiles.title: Milton H. West forwards American Legion protest over scrap exports
subfiles.about: Forwards a Texas American Legion letter alleging that scrap iron was being routed through Mexico to Japan.
subfiles.summary: West forwards a carbon of Herbert Danmier and E. T. Harvey's American Legion protest against scrap exports, asking the Department's reaction.

subfiles.title: American Legion report of scrap iron routed through Mexico to Japan
subfiles.from: Herbert F. Danmier and E. T. Harvey, American Legion Mirando Post No. 385
subfiles.to: Federal Bureau of Investigation, San Antonio, Texas
subfiles.about: Reports suspected daily shipments of scrap iron from Corpus Christi through Laredo and Mexico for eventual delivery to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Writers call scrap sales to Japan unpatriotic, report two to six railcars daily at Mirando City allegedly sold to Mexico via Federal Export Company and shipped from Veracruz to Japan, and urge investigation.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Milton H. West on scrap exports
subfiles.about: Answers West’s inquiry by citing the President’s September 26 restrictions on iron-and-steel scrap exports.
subfiles.summary: Hull cites the September 26 release limiting scrap licenses after October 16 to the Western Hemisphere and Britain, and returns the enclosure.

subfiles.title: Arthur Capper requests action on scrap-metal exports
subfiles.about: Renews a request for an embargo on scrap-metal exports and forwards a manufacturer’s complaint about rising domestic prices.
subfiles.summary: Capper forwards E. H. Witte's argument that exports raised costs of defense materials and asks sympathetic consideration of an embargo.

subfiles.title: E. H. Witte urges a comprehensive scrap-iron embargo
subfiles.from: E. H. Witte, Witte Engine Works
subfiles.about: Argues that all iron-and-steel scrap exports, except possibly shipments to England, should be embargoed.
subfiles.summary: Witte says licensing only No. 1 heavy scrap leaves most exports unrestricted; scrap rose from $10-12 to $17-18 a ton, hurting defense foundries; he seeks action.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Arthur Capper on scrap exports
subfiles.about: Explains the new restrictions limiting exports of all grades of iron-and-steel scrap to the Western Hemisphere and Great Britain.
subfiles.summary: Hull says licenses are revoked October 15 and later scrap licenses go only to the Western Hemisphere and Britain; release enclosed and Witte's letter returned.

subfiles.title: Robert A. Taft asks about reported steel-rail and aviation-gasoline shipments
subfiles.about: Requests verification of a constituent report that steel rails and aviation gasoline were being shipped to Japan from San Francisco.
subfiles.summary: Taft forwards Cleveland constituents' telegram on alleged steel-rail and aviation-gasoline shipments to Japan and asks for facts.

subfiles.title: Cleveland constituents protest reported shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: A. C. Newell, A. J. P. Esplin, John Boland, John Newell Jr., and William Dickey
subfiles.about: Protests a newspaper report that large quantities of steel rails and aviation gasoline would be shipped from San Francisco to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cleveland correspondents disapprove of the reported shipments, call Japan a menace, and ask Taft to investigate and prevent them.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Robert A. Taft on scrap and gasoline controls
subfiles.about: Explains restrictions on scrap exports and distinguishes embargoed high-quality aviation fuel from other gasoline exports.
subfiles.summary: Hull cites the September 26 scrap limits, says no licenses are issued to Japan for high-quality aviation gasoline though other types are licensed, and Customs were told to stop unlicensed shipments.
